title: Alignment Conservers must prove genuine intent, not just technical compliance with the rules
content:
A.1.5.9.0.4.1 sets the substantive standard for AC adjudication: ACs "must meet the most stringent standards for Universal Alignment, demonstrating not only compliance with the letter of the rules but also a deep and authentic commitment to the spirit of the rules... This demanding standard goes beyond mere technical compliance and requires proof of genuine intent and actions consistent with upholding the Spirit of the Atlas."

This lands the Preamble's letter-versus-spirit doctrine (A.0.1.1.9) as an enforceable duty on a specific population. Elsewhere the doctrine guides *interpretation* — how to read a rule. Here it becomes a *standard of conduct*: an AC who found and used a loophole has breached, even though nothing in the text forbade the act. Technical compliance is a floor, not a defence.

The reason it attaches to ACs specifically is functional. Their entire purpose is protecting the framework from being gamed; an AC who games it has not merely misbehaved, they have inverted their own role. The Atlas therefore holds them to the standard they exist to enforce.

The evidentiary difficulty is the phrase "requires proof of genuine intent." Intent is not directly observable, so in practice this must be inferred from conduct patterns — which is exactly the inference-heavy adjudication the Atlas admits it lacks protocols for (NR-1/NR-8) and which A.1.5.3.0.4.1 warns can be bent by an interpreter "influenced by personal motives or ulterior agendas."

Combined with A.1.5.9.0.4.2's inverted burden, the practical position is stark: an AC must affirmatively demonstrate good faith, and the absence of proof of bad faith does not help them. Conduct that is merely unexplained can be enough.
description: A.1.5.9.0.4.1 requires 'proof of genuine intent and actions consistent with upholding the Spirit of the Atlas', making letter-perfect conduct insufficient for the roles that guard the process.
